Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) -- Thirty-eight years ago, Joseph McGinty Nichol was a boy in Kalamazoo, Michigan, playing with toy robots. Many of the robots in "Terminator Salvation" are real machines, which increased realism, the cast says. Today "McG," as he is better known, builds and blows up real robots. The prominent filmmaker is the driving force behind one of the season's summer blockbusters, "Terminator Salvation," which is filled with very expensive and very explosive robots. The choice to use real robots when possible, instead of CGI (computer generated images), was deliberate, McG said. According to the director and the film's stars, the decision to use real machines was a testament to the growing sophistication of the moviegoing public, whom they believe can "feel" the difference between actors standing in front of a green screen versus actors interacting with the real thing. It was also done in honor of the legendary special effects supervisor, four-time Oscar winner Stan Winston ("Jurassic Park," the other "Terminator" films), who passed away during filming last year.  Watch the robots in action » . The director and three of his cast members -- Christian Bale, Bryce Dallas Howard and Anton Yelchin -- took a time out with CNN to explain why gravity and singed eyebrows both played a role in "Terminator Salvation." Bryce Dallas Howard: That was something that was really important to McG ...  when an audience member sees this film, that they can actually feel what's occurring. I think that audiences are very savvy now. We can feel when something is CGI and that's no disrespect to CGI -- we couldn't do this movie without it -- but, whenever possible, in the tradition of Sam Winston, he wanted to build the robots. So a lot of what you see is real. McG: And if you drop something, we've spent our whole lives watching physics in play, and if you say, just have the CGI do that, people can tell something's off, and it releases you from being involved in the picture. So, we built all the robots, we built all the sets, we blew them up for real, a great many of us lost our eyebrows! Christian Bale: It was kind of comical at times because something that's meant to be so intimidating was actually surrounded by five guys with these kind of puppet rods I had to blank out or I would start laughing. But, the end result is something really formidable and you know, really iconic in movie history. Anton Yelchin: Now I'm obsessed with the robots! I'm so [annoyed] that this guy or whoever it is that's in charge of it wouldn't let me have one!

outputs.L1:
**LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) —** Thirty-eight years ago, Joseph McGinty Nichol was a boy in Kalamazoo, Michigan, playing with toy robots. Today, “McG,” as he is better known, builds and blows up real ones.

The prominent filmmaker is the driving force behind one of the summer season’s blockbusters, *Terminator Salvation*, a film filled with extremely expensive—and highly explosive—robots. Many of those robots are real machines, a choice the cast says heightened the film’s realism.

McG said the decision to use real robots whenever possible, rather than CGI (computer-generated imagery), was deliberate. According to the director and the film’s stars, it reflects the growing sophistication of moviegoers, who they believe can “feel” the difference between actors performing in front of a green screen and those interacting with something tangible.

The approach also honored legendary special-effects supervisor and four-time Oscar winner Stan Winston—known for *Jurassic Park* and the other *Terminator* films—who died during filming last year.

**Watch the robots in action »**

The director and three cast members—Christian Bale, Bryce Dallas Howard and Anton Yelchin—took time out to explain to CNN how gravity and singed eyebrows both played a role in *Terminator Salvation*.

**Bryce Dallas Howard:** “That was something that was really important to McG: When an audience member sees this film, they should actually be able to feel what’s occurring. I think audiences are very savvy now. We can feel when something is CGI, and that’s no disrespect to CGI—we couldn’t have made this movie without it—but, whenever possible, in the tradition of Stan Winston, he wanted to build the robots. So, a lot of what you see is real.”

**McG:** “We’ve spent our whole lives watching physics at play. If you say, ‘Just have the CGI do that,’ people can tell something is off, and it takes them out of the picture. So we built all the robots, built all the sets and blew them up for real. A great many of us lost our eyebrows!”

**Christian Bale:** “It was kind of comical at times because something that was meant to be so intimidating was actually surrounded by five guys holding these puppet rods. I had to block them out, or I would start laughing. But the end result is something truly formidable and, you know, really iconic in movie history.”

**Anton Yelchin:** “Now I’m obsessed with the robots! I’m so [annoyed] that this guy—or whoever is in charge—wouldn’t let me have one!”
outputs.L2:
LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — In Kalamazoo, Michigan, 38 years ago, a young Joseph McGinty Nichol played with miniature robots. Now widely known as McG, he makes full-sized machines—and destroys them on camera.

The filmmaker spearheaded “Terminator Salvation,” one of the summer season’s major blockbusters, featuring costly robots and large-scale explosions. Cast members said many of the machines shown in the film were physically built, adding a greater sense of authenticity.

McG explained that the production intentionally relied on practical robots rather than computer-generated imagery whenever feasible. He and the movie’s stars said modern audiences are perceptive enough to sense the distinction between performers working against green screens and those reacting to tangible objects.

The approach also paid tribute to celebrated special-effects supervisor Stan Winston, the four-time Academy Award winner known for “Jurassic Park” and the previous “Terminator” movies. Winston died the year before, while “Terminator Salvation” was being filmed.

Director McG and actors Christian Bale, Bryce Dallas Howard and Anton Yelchin spoke with CNN about how real-world physics—and even scorched eyebrows—shaped the production.

Howard said McG strongly wanted viewers to experience the action as if it were genuinely happening. In her view, today’s audiences quickly recognize CGI. She stressed that this was not criticism of digital effects, which were essential to making the movie, but said McG followed Winston’s practical-effects tradition by constructing robots whenever possible. As a result, much of what appears onscreen physically existed.

McG added that people have observed gravity and motion throughout their lives, so they notice when digitally created objects behave unnaturally. Such inconsistencies can pull viewers out of the story. For that reason, the production built the robots and sets and carried out actual explosions—costing numerous crew members their eyebrows.

Bale recalled that filming could sometimes be amusing. A robot intended to look terrifying might be operated by five people holding puppeteering rods, which he had to ignore to avoid laughing. Nevertheless, he said the finished creation appeared genuinely imposing and belonged to an iconic part of cinema history.

Yelchin said the experience left him fixated on the robots. He was frustrated that whoever controlled them refused to let him keep one.
outputs.L3:
Director Joseph “McG” Nichol relied on real robots whenever possible while making *Terminator Salvation*, believing that physical machines would give the film a greater sense of realism. McG and the cast felt that modern audiences can often distinguish between practical effects and scenes in which actors perform primarily against green screens.

The decision also served as a tribute to legendary special-effects supervisor Stan Winston, who died during the film’s production. Winston was renowned for creating many of the franchise’s iconic machines, and using practical robots helped honor his artistic legacy.

Actress Bryce Dallas Howard acknowledged that computer-generated imagery remained essential to a film of this scale. However, she emphasized that having physical robots on set allowed both the actors and the audience to experience the action more authentically. McG similarly argued that real objects naturally follow recognizable laws of physics, including weight, movement, and momentum. When CGI fails to reproduce those qualities convincingly, it can disrupt the audience’s immersion. By combining practical machines with digital effects, the filmmakers aimed to create a more tangible and believable world.
outputs.L4:
For *Terminator Salvation*, director McG sought to make the conflict between humans and machines feel as tangible as possible. Rather than relying exclusively on computer-generated imagery, the production combined CGI with practical effects, including full-scale robotic creations, physical sets, and real explosions. This approach allowed the actors to respond to objects and events that were actually present during filming, creating more convincing interactions and giving the action a stronger sense of weight and danger.

The use of practical machines also served as a tribute to Stan Winston, the celebrated special-effects artist whose work helped define the visual identity of the *Terminator* series. Winston died during the film’s production, but his influence remained central to its design philosophy. By preserving the franchise’s tradition of detailed, physically constructed creatures and robots while supplementing them with modern digital effects, McG aimed to honor Winston’s legacy rather than replace it.

McG and members of the cast argued that audiences can often sense when movement, impact, or gravity does not behave naturally. Even highly polished CGI may feel artificial if the physics are unconvincing or if performers have nothing real to react to. Full-size machines and practical explosions therefore gave the actors concrete reference points and helped produce more instinctive performances.

The filmmakers saw this blend of practical and digital techniques as a sign of respect for contemporary viewers. As audiences become more familiar with sophisticated visual effects, they also become better at recognizing imagery that lacks realism. Using real machinery wherever possible—and employing CGI to extend or enhance what had been filmed—was intended to make *Terminator Salvation* more immersive, believable, and faithful to the tactile power of the earlier films.

Los Angeles, California, is one of the world’s most famous cities. Located along the Pacific Coast, it is known for its sunny climate, cultural diversity, entertainment industry, and distinctive neighborhoods.
